Cycling and the promotion of health
abs: In the debate about the role of cycling and the grounds for investing public funds for its provision, the focus has been on reducing the risk of injury. Little attention has been paid to its scope for promoting public health. An overview of the subject drawn from a recently published report indicates that the scope is so considerable as to far outweigh the damage to health in cycle accidents (Hillman,M Cycling towards health and safety published by Oxford University Press, 1992). The objectives of policy on health, as well as on environment, energy conservation, equity and economy, would be furthered by enabling much wider use of the bicycle than is made at present. Evidence on health benefits provides further justification for cycling deserving pride of place in the mechanised transport hierarchy - that is going well beyond simply treating it as a mode of transport worthy of some consideration in the allocation of public resources. Health promotion can be added to the bicycle's virtues in terms of social equity, independence for the user, door-to- door convenience, flexibility, and speed on the majority of journeys that most people currently make. In addition, cycle use contributes hardly any of the adverse impacts on health of car use - increasing danger, pollution, noise and community severance. Opting for grant‐maintained status: A study of policymaking in education
abs: The grant-maintained (GM) schools policy, which is one of a number of government initiatives aimed at reforming and restructuring state education, was announced in the Conservative party manifesto for the 1987 general election and subsequently incorporated into the 1988 Education Reform Act (ERA). Operating as autonomous institutions, outside the control of the local education authorities (LEAs) from which they had elected to 'opt out', GM schools obtain their funds direct from the Department for Education (DfE). The GM schools policy was, and remains, especially relevant to contemporary policy making in education because its chief purposes to diversify further school provision, to increase competition between schools, and to enhance parental choice are central elements of government thinking about the future shape and direction of education provision. The policy was represented by its advocates as an opportunity to 'take education out of the hands of planners and return it to parents where it belongs and a means by which educational standards would be improved and school provision diversified. Its opponents disputed whether it would extend choice to all families, while others saw it as 'preserving grammar schools and extending selection by the back door'. These competing claims about the policy provide the basis for our empirical investigation of the extent to which the intentions of its architects and the predictions of its critics have been realised. In examining the development of the GM schools policy and its impact on education provision in England, we drew on a variety of documentary sources and on recorded interviews with samples of those involved in the policy's formulation and implementation. We also interviewed local authority officials about their perceptions of, and responses to, GM schools
